concepts.name: Private fields require a compatible receiver

questions.prompt: `const proto={x:1}; const obj=Object.create(proto); obj.x=2;` What does proto.x become?

choices.text: It becomes undefined; assigning obj.x removes the inherited property.
It becomes 1 only until obj.x is next read, then the values synchronize.
It remains 1; the normal writable inherited property is shadowed on obj.
It becomes 2; assignments always update the object where lookup found the property.

questions.explanation: A normal assignment to an inherited writable data property creates an own property on the receiver. It does not update that property on the prototype.

sources.title: ECMAScript: Fundamental Objects
sources.claim: Object.create establishes a prototype reference and Object.hasOwn tests for an own property without accepting inherited properties.

questions.prompt: An object reads `x` from its prototype but has no own x. What does `Object.hasOwn(obj, "x")` indicate?

choices.text: False, because Object.hasOwn excludes all data properties as well as inherited ones.
False, because the readable property is inherited rather than own.
True, because every readable property counts as an own property.
True, because property lookup copies inherited values onto the receiver.

questions.explanation: Own-property checks distinguish direct properties from inherited ones. A successful read does not imply ownership.

questions.prompt: A property is defined with a getter. What does reading that property normally do?

choices.text: It invokes the getter rather than returning a stored data-property value.
It returns the getter function itself without invoking it.
It invokes the setter because reads and writes share one accessor slot.
It caches the first return value and skips all later getter calls automatically.

questions.explanation: An accessor read calls its getter. Getter values are not automatically cached, and a setter handles writes rather than reads.

questions.prompt: A class method reads `this.#value`. Calling the method with an unrelated plain object as this fails. Why?

choices.text: The method requires every receiver to have a public property named value.
Private fields are stored as ordinary string keys but cannot be read through this.
All detached class methods fail even when called with their original instance.
The receiver lacks the private field brand required by that class.

questions.explanation: Private access checks the compatible receiver brand. A same-looking public property cannot supply it; a correctly supplied original instance remains compatible.

sources.title: ECMAScript: Functions and Classes
sources.claim: Functions retain lexical environments; arrow functions use lexical this, and class private fields require their declaring brand.

questions.prompt: A writable own property shadows the same name on a prototype. After deleting only the own property, what can a read do?

choices.text: Recreate the deleted own property before consulting the prototype.
Throw because deleting an own property disables later prototype lookup.
Find the still-existing property through the prototype chain.
Return undefined because delete removes that name from the whole chain.

questions.explanation: Removing an own property can expose an inherited property. Delete does not recursively remove names from the prototype chain.

questions.prompt: An own property has the value undefined. How does its existence compare with a missing own property?

choices.text: The property exists only while a getter for it is actively executing.
The property can still be own even though its value is undefined.
The property is automatically removed when its value becomes undefined.
The property becomes inherited as soon as its value becomes undefined.

questions.explanation: Property existence and value are distinct. Undefined can be the value of a present data property.

questions.prompt: A plain object uses a prototype with writable data properties. Which lookup claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assignment to an inherited writable data property normally shadows it.
Own properties can shadow inherited names.
A missing own property can be found on the prototype.
Deleting an own property always deletes its inherited counterpart.
Reading a property copies it permanently onto the receiver.

questions.explanation: a: The receiver can get an own data property instead of mutating the prototype. b: Lookup considers a matching own property before the prototype. c: Ordinary lookup follows the prototype chain. d: Deletion targets the object own property. e: Lookup does not itself create a new own property.

questions.prompt: A review distinguishes ownership from values. Which claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An own property may contain undefined.
An inherited property can be readable without being own.
A successful read proves the property is own.
Assigning undefined necessarily deletes the property.
Every inherited property is copied when an object is created.

questions.explanation: a: Undefined is a valid stored value. b: Read lookup and own-property testing are different operations. c: The prototype chain can supply the value. d: Assignment and deletion are separate operations. e: The prototype is referenced rather than copied into all own slots.

questions.prompt: An object exposes data and accessor properties. Which descriptor claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Writable controls reassignment of data properties.
An accessor can define a setter for assignments.
Every getter result is automatically memoized by the language.
A data descriptor must include a getter and setter.
A getter can run code on a property read.

questions.explanation: a: It is a data descriptor attribute. b: The setter handles writes when present. c: Each read may invoke the getter again. d: Data and accessor descriptors are distinct descriptor forms. e: Accessor reads invoke the getter.

questions.prompt: A class uses private fields. Which receiver claims hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Any object with the same public shape can satisfy private access.
An unrelated this argument can cause private access to throw.
Private fields become enumerable string-keyed properties.
A method needs a receiver with its declaring private brand.
A public property with the same spelling does not supply that brand.

questions.explanation: a: Structural public similarity does not establish the private brand. b: The brand check can fail for that receiver. c: They do not appear as ordinary enumerable public properties. d: Private access checks the receiver compatibility. e: Private names are distinct from string-keyed public properties.
